summary: Gives advice on when it is safe to begin sending data on a label switched path set up with RSVP-TE. Each node is programmed as signaling messages are processed, so data sent too early can be lost or misdelivered. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Setting up a path involves two things happening at once: messages telling each router where to send traffic, and each router actually programming itself to do so. This RFC works out, by reading the existing standards, exactly when it is safe to start pushing data.

subtitle: When it is safe to start pushing data down a path that RSVP-TE has just set up.

tldr.problem: Setting up a labelled path involves messages telling each router where to forward traffic, and each router actually programming itself to do so, and the two do not finish at the same moment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reads the RSVP-TE and GMPLS standards together and works out, for each kind of path, the point at which the sender can start transmitting without losing or misdelivering data.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new procedures. It gives implementers the rule they need, and gives equipment vendors a way to interpret the setup times they quote.

today: RFC 6383 is an Informational document published in September 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no new procedures; it reads the existing RSVP-TE and GMPLS documents together and says what they imply about when data may safely start flowing.

sections.title: When Is It Safe to Start Sending Data
sections.content:
RSVP has been extended to support traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks, so that signalling exchanges can establish label switched paths across nodes and links to give an end-to-end data path. Each node is programmed with cross-connect information as the signalling messages are processed, and that information tells the node how to forward the data it receives. In some technologies this means configuring physical devices; in others it means exchanging commands between components inside the node.

The ends of a path need to know when it is safe to start sending data, and safe has two meanings here. The first is that the sender must know the data path has been fully established, with the cross-connects set up and any old, incorrect forwarding instructions removed, so the data will arrive where it is meant to. The second is that in optical technologies the lasers must not be switched on until the correct cross-connects are in place, so that service personnel are not put at risk. Every router along the path has the same question in a different form: when should it program its data plane relative to sending and receiving control-plane messages.

This document clarifies and summarises the RSVP-TE exchanges in relation to programming cross-connects, for unidirectional and bidirectional paths. It defines no new procedures or protocol extensions and defers completely to the documents it cites. Bidirectional paths are supported only in GMPLS. The clarifications may also be used to interpret LSP establishment performance figures: the dynamic provisioning metrics in RFC 5814 have to be read in the context of LSP setup times, not just control message exchange times, which are only one component of the whole establishment.

Implementations could gain a lot by identifying each router that forwards the Path or Resv message before programming its cross-connect, and pipelining the work to cut the total setup time. But the document is careful about how far it can go: it is not possible to make definitive statements about how much pipelining is safe, because a node cannot know much without first probing the network, which would defeat the point. With path length and node behaviour introducing so many variables, the ingress may end up limited to a very pessimistic view for safety. Nor is it likely that an implementation would give a full and frank description of how long it takes to program and stabilise its cross-connects.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a path involves two things happening at once: messages telling each router where to send traffic, and each router actually programming itself to do so. This RFC works out exactly when it is safe to start pushing data.

sections.title: What a Cross-Connect Is
sections.content:
A cross-connection here means the data forwarding instructions installed, or programmed, at a network node or switch.

In packet MPLS networks this is usually the Incoming Label Map and the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry, sometimes treated together as entries in the Label Forwarding Information Base. Where there is admission control and resource reservation associated with the forwarding path, such as the allocation of data buffers, that can be treated as part of the cross-connect programming process, because the path will not be able to forward data in the agreed manner until the resources are correctly allocated and reserved.

In non-packet networks, such as time-division multiplexing or optical switching, the cross-connect may be an electronic cross-connect array or a transparent optical device such as a microelectromechanical system. In every case the concept is the same: the instructions programmed into the forwarding plane, so that data arriving for the path on one port can be forwarded correctly out of another.
sections.plainLanguage: The cross-connect is the router's own forwarding table entry: the instruction that says what to do with data that arrives carrying a particular label.

sections.title: Unidirectional MPLS-TE Paths
sections.content:
RFC 3209 describes the RSVP-TE signalling and processing for packet-based MPLS-TE networks, where paths are unidirectional by definition. Its Section 4.1.1.1 describes what a node does before sending the Resv message to its upstream neighbour: it sends the new Label object as part of the Resv message to the previous hop, and it should be prepared to forward packets carrying the assigned label before it sends the Resv.

So the cross-connect should be in place before the Resv goes out, because traffic may arrive at the node before the node sends the Resv. That is plainly advisable, since the upstream routers might otherwise complete their cross-connections more quickly and encourage the ingress to start transmitting, with the risk that the node that sent the Resv early could not forward the data it received and would have to drop it, or might even send it along the wrong path because of stale cross-connect information.

The SHOULD in that text leaves room for an implementation that sends a Resv before it is ready to receive and forward data. That might happen because the internal construction of the node means the control-plane components cannot easily tell when the cross-connect has been installed, or because the implementation knows it will be slow and does not want to hold up the establishment of the path. In the latter case the implementation is choosing to pipeline the cross-connect programming with the protocol exchange, taking a gamble that other upstream routers will also take some time to process, and that it will in any case be some time before the ingress actually starts sending. Such a node must also have a mechanism to report a failure to chase the Resv message, using a PathErr, if the pipelined cross-connect processing fails.
sections.plainLanguage: For a plain packet path, the rule is simple: a router must be ready to forward the label before it tells the router upstream. Otherwise data could arrive before the router is ready, and be dropped or sent down the wrong path.

sections.title: GMPLS: Suggested Labels, Bidirectional Paths and Admin Status
sections.content:
GMPLS extends RSVP-TE signalling for networks of different technologies, so the same signalling can be used in MPLS packet switching, layer two networks such as Ethernet, Frame Relay and ATM, time-division multiplexing networks such as SONET and SDH, wavelength division multiplexing networks, and fibre switched networks. The optical technologies bring the second meaning of safe into play: there is a physical safety issue, so the lasers should not be enabled until the cross-connects are correctly in place.

Unidirectional processing is as before, except for the Suggested_Label object, which lets an upstream router suggest to its downstream neighbour the label that should be used for forward-direction data by including it on a Path message. The purpose is to help the downstream router choose a label, but it also lets the upstream router pipeline its cross-connect programming with the signalling, so the cross-connect may be in place before the signalling has completed, that is, before a Resv carrying a Label object has been received upstream.

Three pieces of the standards say when it is safe to start sending, and they agree. Section 3.4 of RFC 3471 says an ingress node should not transmit data traffic on a suggested label until the downstream node passes a label upstream, so the ingress may safely start when it receives a label in a Resv message. Section 2.5 of RFC 3473 confirms it. And Section 4.1.1.1 of RFC 3209 says the node should be prepared to forward packets carrying the assigned label before it sends the Resv, where the word prior is crucial: each transit and egress node must finish making its cross-connects before it sends the Resv upstream. Taken together, the ingress must not start transmitting until it has both received a Resv and programmed its own cross-connect.

A bidirectional path is established with one signalling exchange: a Path from ingress to egress and a Resv from egress to ingress. The path itself is two sets of forwarding state, one for the forward direction and one for the reverse. The forward direction works exactly as in the unidirectional case. For the reverse direction, an Upstream_Label object travels in the Path message from each router to its downstream neighbour, telling the downstream router which label to use for data heading back upstream. The downstream router confirms the label when it sends its Resv; there is no explicit confirmation of the label in the Resv, but if the label was not acceptable the downstream router would return a PathErr instead. The Upstream_Label object must indicate a label that is valid for forwarding at the time the Path message is sent, which means it is safe for the sending router to receive data and that it will forward it correctly, not that the label is available to be cross-connected. RFC 3473 also says that terminator nodes process Path messages as usual, with the exception that the upstream label can immediately be used to transport data upstream towards the initiator.

From this the RFC deduces three things. A router must not wait for a Resv before programming the cross-connect for the reverse direction; it must be ready to receive data from the moment the egress finishes processing the Path message, before it sends a Resv back upstream. A router may expect to start receiving reverse direction data as soon as it sends a Path message for a bidirectional path. And it may make assumptions about the time lag between sending the Path and the message reaching and being processed by the egress, and use that lag to pipeline the programming of its cross-connect.

ResvConf. The ResvConf message is used in standard RSVP to let the ingress confirm to the egress that the Resv was received and what bandwidth was reserved. In RSVP-TE and GMPLS the bandwidth is not expected to change along the path, so its purpose is reduced to confirming that the path was established. The egress may request one by including a Resv_Confirm object in its Resv, and the ingress can then reply. This would give the egress a doubly secure way to be sure the reverse direction data path is in place, but the RFC calls it excessive given the definitions above, and it would delay setup by one end-to-end message propagation cycle. The generation of the ResvConf is not guaranteed either, and many, if not most, GMPLS implementations neither request nor send it, so relying on it is not recommended.

Administrative status. GMPLS offers an additional tool. The Admin_Status object lets an ingress set up a path in an administratively down state, in which it is assumed the path exists, with the cross-connects all in place, but no data is transmitted, so in optical systems the lasers are off. The same object allows the path to be put into a testing state, which lets the connectivity be checked without exchanging user data: in an optical system a data continuity test, and in a packet network a connection verification exchange such as the in-band Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification. Once connectivity is verified the path can be put into active mode and user data can start. These processes matter most where the control-plane processors are physically separate from the data-plane cross-connects, so that successful control-plane signalling cannot be taken as evidence of correct data-plane programming.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS adds two things. A label can be suggested in advance so the setup can be pipelined, and a path can be held in a state where the switches are connected but the lasers are off, so the link can be tested before anyone sends data over it.

sections.title: What This Means for Performance Figures
sections.content:
How quickly routers handle and pass on control-plane messages and program their cross-connects varies a lot from device to device, according to the switching technology, the control-plane connectivity and the implementation, and those factors influence how quickly a path can be established. Different applications have different requirements for setup speed, which matters especially in recovery scenarios. Providers considering MPLS-TE or GMPLS equipment need a good benchmark for its performance, and vendors need to be compared on a level playing field.

RFC 5814 defines a series of performance metrics for evaluating dynamic LSP provisioning, and any use of them has to be careful about what is being measured. It is not enough to know that the control-plane message has been processed and forwarded: the cross-connect must be in place before the path can be used. So care is needed to ensure that devices really follow the procedures clarified here, and are not simply forwarding control-plane messages with the intention of programming the cross-connects in the background.
sections.plainLanguage: When a vendor quotes how fast it sets up a path, check what is being timed. A router that answers messages quickly but programs its switches afterwards has not finished the job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says it defines no network behaviour and neither introduces nor seeks to solve any security issues. It notes, though, that a clear understanding of when to start sending data may reduce the risk of data being accidentally delivered to the wrong place, or of people being hurt.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing about security is specified here. The one remark is that knowing the right moment to start sending reduces the chance of data going somewhere it should not, and of hurting the people who maintain the network.

items.title: Delivery, not misdelivery
items.text: The sender must know the whole data path is ready and that no stale forwarding instructions are left behind.

items.title: Laser safety
items.text: In optical systems the laser must not be switched on until the cross-connects are correct.

items.title: Pipelining
items.text: Programming the cross-connect while the messages are still travelling saves setup time.

items.title: Reporting failure
items.text: A router that pipelines must report a failure with a PathErr if the cross-connect does not work.
